prompt: By the lesson, what is the main reason an architect keeps writing code?
hint: An instrument whose readings drift.

choices.text: To stay the best programmer on the team
choices.why: That is the second wrong picture the lesson opens with; heroics are not the point.

choices.text: Calibration
choices.why: Right: staying in touch with what a design costs to build, so the next one is priced correctly.

choices.text: To finish features the team has no time for
choices.why: That puts the architect on the critical path, which the next section rules out.

choices.text: To keep a job title that includes engineering
choices.why: Status is the first wrong picture; the reason is about the quality of the designs.

prompt: Renata estimated the outbox change at two weeks and Bruno's team at six. What did her afternoon pairing with Ícaro show?
hint: A 41-minute test suite, a newer framework, a review on Thursdays.

choices.text: That the team was padding to protect itself
choices.why: That was her first assumption, and the afternoon disproved it.

choices.text: That the outbox pattern was the wrong design
choices.why: The design was sound; it was priced wrongly.

choices.text: That Ícaro needed more training in transactions
choices.why: Renata was the one who spent an hour reading about the framework's transactions.

choices.text: That the team's number was calibrated, hers not
choices.why: Right: the friction she had stopped feeling was real, and the team's six weeks counted it.

prompt: In Fowler's "Who Needs an Architect?", what is most important in the work of *Architectus oryzus*?
hint: The other species makes the decisions itself.

choices.text: Making the important decisions for the developers
choices.why: That describes *Architectus reloadus*, the species Fowler contrasts it with.

choices.text: Writing the architecture document before the project starts
choices.why: Fowler's picture is of somebody inside the project, programming in the morning and in a requirements session in the afternoon.

choices.text: Reviewing and approving each design
choices.why: Approval as a gate is closer to deciding for others than to collaborating.

choices.text: Mentoring the developers
choices.why: Right: so that they handle more of the important issues themselves.

prompt: In Gregor Hohpe's architect elevator, where is the value of the architect's work?
hint: Between the penthouse and the engine room.

choices.text: In the penthouse, where strategy is set
choices.why: An architect who stops there has nothing to carry up.

choices.text: In the engine room, where the systems run
choices.why: Staying below loses the people who decide; the engine room alone is the engineer's job.

choices.text: In the ride between the two
choices.why: Right: carrying what the engine room knows up, and the decisions down in a usable form.

choices.text: In the meeting rooms on the middle floors
choices.why: The metaphor has two ends, and the work is moving between them.

prompt: Carreto's diagram shows Payments calling Tracking through an API, yet a schema change in Tracking broke payouts. What would reading the code have shown?
hint: The real dependencies.

choices.text: A direct read of the other service's tables, outside the API
choices.why: Right: added during an incident two years earlier, and invisible on the slide.

choices.text: That the API between the two services had no version number
choices.why: Versioning the API would not have protected a dependency that does not go through it.

choices.text: That Tracking deploys more often than Payments
choices.why: Deploy frequency does not explain how a schema change reached Payments.

choices.text: That the two teams disagree about the message format
choices.why: No message is involved: the break came through the database.

prompt: Fowler's architect who makes all the important decisions personally is *Architectus* ___.
hint: The species that is not *oryzus*.

prompt: A design is sound but priced at a third of what it will cost to build. Why does the lesson call that wrong "in a slower way"?
hint: Who pays the difference, and when?

choices.text: Approved at a cost it won't meet, the team pays the gap
choices.why: Right: the error surfaces during the build, as time spent by people who did not choose the design.

choices.text: It slows the system down in production, where users notice
choices.why: The design itself is sound; the problem is in the estimate, not in run-time behaviour.

choices.text: It takes longer to review than a correctly priced design
choices.why: Review time is not the cost the lesson means; the build is.

choices.text: Its bugs appear months later
choices.why: A mispriced design can be bug-free; the damage is in the plan.

prompt: An architect has two uninterrupted half-days a week and takes a story estimated at four days of focused work. How many weeks of elapsed time will it take?
hint: Convert the days to half-days first.

prompt: By the lesson, what decides whether a piece of code is suitable for an architect to write?
hint: The shape of the work, not its importance.

choices.text: How difficult it is
choices.why: The hardest piece is the one most likely to be on the critical path.

choices.text: How important it is to the business
choices.why: Importance says nothing about whether a release waits on the architect's calendar.

choices.text: Whether it fits gaps in the week and blocks nobody
choices.why: Right: the rule is off the critical path, because an architect's week is full of interruptions.

choices.text: Whether it uses the newest technology the team has
choices.why: Novelty is a résumé reason, which lesson 2 already warned about.

prompt: The hardest part of a migration is the one where Renata's experience matters most. What does the lesson say she should do with it?
hint: The owner stays the owner.

choices.text: Take it herself, since nobody else knows as much
choices.why: It is the piece most likely on the critical path, and the team learns least where there is most to learn.

choices.text: Write a detailed design and hand it over
choices.why: Handing over a design keeps her outside the code, where the calibration does not happen.

choices.text: Leave it alone so the team grows on its own
choices.why: Staying away wastes the experience; pairing uses it without taking the work.

choices.text: Pair on it with its owner
choices.why: Right: the experience is used, the owner keeps it, and nobody waits on her calendar.

prompt: Match each kind of code to what it is.
hint: One is thrown away, one is used by a person, one runs end to end, one fails the build.

pairs.right: a few days of code that answer a question, then deleted
a rough version a person uses, to learn whether the idea works
one small function running through every part of the design
a check that fails the build when a rule is broken

right_distractors: the release's last story, done in spare hours

prompt: Renata's walking skeleton found in its first afternoon that the provider's sandbox needs an allow-listed IP address. Why does the lesson count that as the skeleton working?
hint: Where do problems that live in connections show up otherwise?

choices.text: A connection problem surfaced on day one, not in week nine
choices.why: Right: exercising every connection once is what moves those surprises to the start.

choices.text: It showed the provider was the wrong choice for instant payout
choices.why: An allow-list is a small configuration change; nothing about it argues against the provider.

choices.text: It gave Paula's team work to do
choices.why: The ticket is a consequence; the value is when it was found.

choices.text: It replaced a spike
choices.why: A skeleton and a spike answer different questions; neither replaced the other here.

prompt: An architect reads pull requests every week. Where does the lesson draw the line?
hint: Comments, or a gate?

choices.text: Reading is a waste once the architect writes code
choices.why: Reading complements writing; it shows how the design is turning out across the system.

choices.text: Reviews belong to the tech leads, so the architect stays out
choices.why: Comments from the architect are welcome; the lesson's objection is to approval as a gate.

choices.text: Comment freely, but do not be each merge's approval
choices.why: Right: an architect who approves each pull request is on the critical path by another route.

choices.text: Read only the pull requests that change the database
choices.why: The lesson says to read where the important decisions live, which is wider than the database.

prompt: What is the lesson's defence against a prototype that works being shipped by accident?
hint: Say what it is, where it lives.

choices.text: Write it in a language the team does not use
choices.why: That makes it harder to learn from, and it says nothing about what happens to it.

choices.text: Label it in the code and README, and agree its fate first
choices.why: Right: the repository's name and the README's first line say what it is, and its end is agreed before it exists.

choices.text: Keep it on the architect's laptop
choices.why: Hiding it stops the team learning from it, which is what a prototype is for.

choices.text: Give it no tests
choices.why: Missing tests do not stop anybody shipping; a label and an agreement do more.

prompt: Renata's coding time disappeared within two months. What brought it back?
hint: Each meeting looked more urgent than a fix nobody was waiting for.

choices.text: Blocked mornings with names, moved rather than deleted
choices.why: Right: time with a name on it is defended the way a commitment is.

choices.text: Coding in the evenings instead
choices.why: That moves the cost to her own time and is the first thing to go in a hard week.

choices.text: Declining meetings with product and finance
choices.why: Those conversations are part of the role; the fix was protecting time beside them.

choices.text: A quarterly week of coding
choices.why: The lesson prefers a fifth of each week, because the instrument drifts between readings.

prompt: Ícaro, two years out of university, asks Renata to rename two functions and to drop a sleep from her test. What does the lesson say she did, and why did it matter?
hint: Review applies upwards.

choices.text: She explained the reasoning behind her names, to teach him
choices.why: Both of his comments were right; defending the names would have made the review a test of rank.

choices.text: She merged it and fixed the names in a later change
choices.why: Going around the review would have shown the team the conventions bind everybody but her.

choices.text: She fixed both and said so in the review
choices.why: Right: the team saw its conventions bind the architect too, and she learnt an agreement that no document recorded.

choices.text: She asked Bruno to review it instead
choices.why: Choosing a more senior reviewer would tell Ícaro his review does not count.

prompt: Which of these are signs, by the lesson, that an architect's calibration has drifted? Choose all that apply.
hint: Five questions, asked once a month.

choices.text: The build time they quote is from last year
choices.why: Yes: every design priced on it is mispriced.

choices.text: They cannot run the system from a clean checkout today
choices.why: Yes: if the local setup moved on without them, so did the code.

choices.text: The team asks them more questions than last year
choices.why: More questions say people value the advice; nothing in that is drift.

choices.text: Their review comments are about naming and formatting alone
choices.why: Yes: that is what is left when the reviewer no longer sees what the change does.

choices.text: They wrote a fitness function last month
choices.why: That is a sign of the habit kept, not of drift.

prompt: An architect spends ten hours a week on a side project in a new language and none in the company's code. By the lesson, are they calibrated?
hint: Calibrated to what?

choices.text: Yes, because ten hours is more than the lesson asks for
choices.why: The amount is beside the point when the hours are spent in a different system.

choices.text: Yes, if the new language is one the company might adopt
choices.why: Even then, it says nothing about this month's test suite or deploy.

choices.text: No: it comes from the code the decisions are about
choices.why: Right: a little in the real system beats a lot elsewhere, for this purpose.

choices.text: No, because architects should not code outside work
choices.why: The lesson welcomes the side project for curiosity; it just does not calibrate.

prompt: Why does the lesson insist that an architect's change reaches production rather than stopping on a branch?
hint: Each stage after the code is part of what a design costs.

choices.text: To raise the architect's count of commits
choices.why: Output is not the aim; the lesson says calibration, not production.

choices.text: Because unfinished branches block the team's merges
choices.why: A stale branch blocks nobody; the loss is what the architect fails to learn.

choices.text: So the team sees the architect is still productive
choices.why: Appearances are not the reason; what the release process teaches is.

choices.text: Tests, review, pipeline and monitoring are part of the cost
choices.why: Right: an abandoned branch teaches the first half-day and nothing after it.

prompt: Put the parts of Renata's walking skeleton in the order a driver's request passes through them.
hint: From the button to the money.
items: One transfer of R$ 1 in the provider's sandbox
trap: The ledger entry comes before the transfer: Payments records what it is about to pay, then asks the provider to pay it.

prompt: An architect at another company takes the core module of a database migration because she knows it best. Five weeks later the team is still waiting for it. Which rule was broken, and what was the alternative?
hint: Her calendar, the team's release.

choices.text: She coded at all; she should have stayed in design reviews
choices.why: The lesson wants architects coding, just not here.

choices.text: The critical path; pairing with the owner was the way
choices.why: Right: her interrupted week turned days of work into weeks of waiting, and pairing would have used her knowledge without that.

choices.text: Calibration; she should have estimated the module first
choices.why: A better estimate would still leave the release waiting on her calendar.

choices.text: Review; the team should have reviewed her design
choices.why: Review was not the problem; who held the critical piece was.

prompt: For the third time this quarter, a team estimates a change at three times what Renata expected. What does the lesson suggest she does first?
hint: Padding or calibrated? Lesson 14 has the question.

choices.text: Ask the team's tech lead to lower the estimate
choices.why: Pressing the number down hides the friction the team is counting.

choices.text: Take her own number to Helena
choices.why: A repeated gap is a sign her instrument may be the one that drifted.

choices.text: Average the two estimates
choices.why: Averaging keeps both errors and explains neither.

choices.text: Ask what would make it take that long, and pair on a piece
choices.why: Right: the answer is either a risk to write down or friction she had stopped feeling.

prompt: As Carreto grows to fifteen teams, Renata will code less. What does the lesson say should stay the same?
hint: An amount, and a place.

choices.text: Her two mornings a week, whatever the size of the company
choices.why: The lesson expects the amount to shrink; what it protects is different.

choices.text: Above zero, and in the system the decisions are about
choices.why: Right: a little in the real system keeps her calibrated as the role leans towards the enterprise level.

choices.text: Pairing with each team in rotation
choices.why: With fifteen teams the rotation would not come round before the calibration fades.

choices.text: Owning one service herself
choices.why: Owning a service puts her on its critical path, the thing the lesson rules out.
